emperor-tenmu.name: Emperor Tenmu
emperor-tenmu.summary: 40th emperor of Japan (c. 630–686), who took the throne after winning the Jinshin War against his nephew and modeled his government on Tang China.

mandu-food.name: Mandu
mandu-food.summary: Korean dumplings that can be steamed, boiled, pan-fried or deep-fried, once part of royal court cuisine and now sold throughout South Korea.

mantou.name: Mantou
mantou.summary: A white, soft steamed bread or bun popular in northern China, sometimes called a Chinese steamed bun, with a name folk etymology links to a tale about Zhuge Liang.

manj.name: Manjū
manj.summary: A traditional Japanese confection, usually a small bun with a sweet filling such as azuki bean paste, made in many shapes and typically steamed or baked.

samurai.name: Samurai
samurai.summary: Japan's professional warrior class in the pre-industrial era, serving noble lords and trained from youth in swordsmanship, archery, horsemanship and Confucian learning.

ryukyu-kingdom.name: Ryukyu Kingdom
ryukyu-kingdom.summary: A kingdom ruling the Ryukyu Islands from 1429 to 1872 as a tributary state of the Ming dynasty, later a vassal of Japan's Satsuma Domain before full annexation in 1879.

awamori.name: Awamori
awamori.summary: A distilled alcoholic beverage unique to Okinawa's Ryukyuan cuisine, traditionally made from rice rather than brewed like sake.

suwa-taisha.name: Suwa Shrine
suwa-taisha.summary: A group of Shinto shrines in Nagano Prefecture, Japan, considered one of the oldest shrines in existence, already standing by the late 7th century.

shinano-province.name: Shinano Province
shinano-province.summary: An old province of Japan, now Nagano Prefecture, whose ancient capital lay near modern-day Matsumoto.

shimotsuke-province.name: Shimotsuke Province
shimotsuke-province.summary: An old province of Japan corresponding to today's Tochigi Prefecture, ranked among the 'great countries' under the Engishiki classification system.

genji-monogatari-emaki.name: Genji Monogatari Emaki
genji-monogatari-emaki.summary: A 12th-century illustrated handscroll depicting The Tale of Genji, the earliest surviving example of its kind and a National Treasure of Japan.

yamato-e.name: Yamato-e
yamato-e.summary: A classical style of Japanese painting developed by the late Heian period, marked by small figures, floating-cloud framing, and narrative or seasonal scenes.

the-tale-of-genji.name: The Tale of Genji
the-tale-of-genji.summary: An early 11th-century work of Japanese literature attributed to the noblewoman Murasaki Shikibu, often called the first novel by a woman to win global recognition; in Japan it holds a stature similar to Shakespeare's works.

murasaki-shikibu.name: Murasaki Shikibu
murasaki-shikibu.summary: Japanese novelist, poet and lady-in-waiting of the Heian court (c. 973 – c. 1014/1025), best known as the author of The Tale of Genji, considered one of the world's first novels.

goryeo-ware.name: Goryeo ware
goryeo-ware.summary: Korean pottery and porcelain, most often celadon greenware, produced during the Goryeo dynasty (918–1392) and prized for its distinctive inlay technique and green color.

goryeo.name: Goryeo
goryeo.summary: Korean kingdom founded in 918 that unified the peninsula and ruled until 1392, giving Korea its name and becoming a golden age of Buddhism and commerce.

nin-war.name: Ōnin War
nin-war.summary: A civil war in Japan from 1467 to 1477, sparked by a dispute between Hosokawa Katsumoto and Yamana Sōzen, that drew in the Ashikaga shogunate and many feudal lords and began the long Sengoku 'Warring States' period.

muromachi-period.name: Muromachi period
muromachi-period.summary: Period of Japanese history from about 1336 to 1573, marked by rule of the Ashikaga shogunate based in Kyoto until its last shogun was driven out by Oda Nobunaga.

sh-koku-ji.name: Shōkoku-ji
sh-koku-ji.summary: Buddhist temple in northern Kyoto founded in 1382 by Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, rebuilt several times over the centuries.

sessh-t-y.name: Sesshū Tōyō
sessh-t-y.summary: Japanese Zen monk and painter (c. 1420-1506) considered a master of ink painting, who blended Chinese influences from a journey to China with a distinctly Japanese Zen style.

tohwas.name: Dohwaseo
tohwas.summary: The Joseon-period Royal Academy of Painting, responsible for producing pictures requested by government offices; originally called Dohwawŏn under the Goryeo dynasty.

tensh-sh-bun.name: Shūbun
tensh-sh-bun.summary: A Japanese Zen Buddhist monk and painter of the Muromachi period, who died around 1444 to 1450.

ban-dainagon-ekotoba.name: Ban Dainagon Ekotoba
ban-dainagon-ekotoba.summary: A late 12th-century Japanese handscroll painting, over 20 metres long, depicting the Ōtemmon Conspiracy of the early Heian period, attributed to the painter Tokiwa Mitsunaga.

gongmin-of-goryeo.name: Gongmin of Goryeo
gongmin-of-goryeo.summary: 31st ruler of Goryeo, reigning from 1351 to 1374 as the second son of King Chungsuk; also known by his Mongolian name, Bayan Temür.

yi-chehy-n.name: Yi Chehyŏn
yi-chehy-n.summary: A Goryeo-era Korean politician, Neo-Confucian scholar, philosopher, writer and poet (1288-1367), and father of a royal consort of King Gongmin.

m-ngke-khan.name: Möngke Khan
m-ngke-khan.summary: The fourth khagan of the Mongol Empire, ruling 1251–1259, who oversaw conquests of Iraq, Syria and the Dali Kingdom; his death without a successor triggered a civil war that split the empire.

kamakura-shogunate.name: Kamakura shogunate
kamakura-shogunate.summary: Japan's feudal military government from 1185 to 1333, founded by Minamoto no Yoritomo and later dominated by the Hōjō clan, which repelled Mongol invasions in 1274 and 1281.

mongol-invasions-of-japan.name: Mongol invasions of Japan
mongol-invasions-of-japan.summary: Two failed attempts by Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty to conquer Japan, in 1274 and 1281, remembered as the origin of the word kamikaze, or divine wind, for the typhoons that wrecked the invasion fleets.

emperor-go-daigo.name: Emperor Go-Daigo
emperor-go-daigo.summary: 96th emperor of Japan (1288–1339) who overthrew the Kamakura shogunate in 1333 and briefly restored imperial rule before being overthrown himself in 1336.

genpei-war.name: Genpei War
genpei-war.summary: A civil war (1180-1185) between Japan's Taira and Minamoto clans that ended with the Taira's downfall and the founding of the Kamakura shogunate.

taira-clan.name: Taira clan
taira-clan.summary: One of the four most powerful clans of Japan's Heian period, defeated by the rival Minamoto clan in the Genpei War of 1180 to 1185.

battle-of-dan-no-ura.name: Battle of Dan-no-ura
battle-of-dan-no-ura.summary: The decisive 1185 naval battle in which Minamoto no Yoshitsune's fleet destroyed the Taira clan, ending the Genpei War; the young Emperor Antoku died among the Taira dead.

minamoto-no-yoshitsune.name: Minamoto no Yoshitsune
minamoto-no-yoshitsune.summary: A samurai commander (c. 1159–1189) of the Minamoto clan and half-brother of Yoritomo, credited as the key figure in the Minamoto's victory over the Taira clan.

minamoto-no-yoritomo.name: Minamoto no Yoritomo
minamoto-no-yoritomo.summary: Founder and first shogun of Japan's Kamakura shogunate (1192–1199), who defeated the Taira clan in the Genpei War and established samurai rule.

ashikaga-shogunate.name: Ashikaga shogunate
ashikaga-shogunate.summary: Japan's feudal military government from 1336 to 1573, also called the Muromachi shogunate, which favored the arts and trade over military control and was ended by Oda Nobunaga.

sengoku-period.name: Sengoku period
sengoku-period.summary: An era of civil war and political fragmentation in Japanese history, conventionally running from the Ōnin War of 1467 to around 1600, during which regional warlords built independent domains.

deokjong-of-goryeo.name: King Deokjong
deokjong-of-goryeo.summary: The 9th king of Korea's Goryeo dynasty (reigned from 1031, died 1034) who fortified the northern frontier and began building a long defensive wall after the Liao dynasty refused his demands.

khitan-people.name: Khitan people
khitan-people.summary: A nomadic East Asian people descended from the Xianbei who founded the Liao dynasty (916–1125) ruling Mongolia, Siberia and northern China, and later the Qara Khitai in Central Asia; the name Cathay derives from theirs.

jurchen-people.name: Jurchen
jurchen-people.summary: Tungusic-speaking peoples of northeastern China who founded the Jin and Qing dynasties; they were renamed Manchus in 1635 by Hong Taiji.

battle-of-bun-ei.name: Battle of Bun'ei
battle-of-bun-ei.summary: The first major Mongol attempt to invade Japan, in October 1274, when a Mongol-led force landed at Hakata Bay after raiding Tsushima and Iki but withdrew after failing to secure a foothold.

tsushima-island.name: Tsushima
tsushima-island.summary: Japanese island midway between Kyushu and the Korean Peninsula, seized during the Mongol invasions of Japan in 1274.

iki-island.name: Iki Island
iki-island.summary: A small Japanese archipelago in the Tsushima Strait, administered as part of Nagasaki Prefecture, with about 28,000 residents living on just four of its many islands.

emperor-go-shirakawa.name: Emperor Go-Shirakawa
emperor-go-shirakawa.summary: 77th emperor of Japan (1127–1192) whose formal reign lasted 1155–1158 but who held effective power for decades afterward, remaining the last truly ruling emperor until 1868.

emperor-sutoku.name: Emperor Sutoku
emperor-sutoku.summary: 75th emperor of Japan (1119–1164), reigning 1123–1142, later regarded as one of the "Three Great Onryō" (vengeful spirits) of Japan.

taira-no-kiyomori.name: Taira no Kiyomori
taira-no-kiyomori.summary: A Japanese military leader who was the de facto ruler of Japan from 1167 until his death in 1181, establishing the country's first samurai-dominated government.

emperor-antoku.name: Emperor Antoku
emperor-antoku.summary: 81st emperor of Japan (1178–1185), a child enthroned by his grandfather Taira no Kiyomori; drowned by his grandmother when the Taira were defeated at Dan-no-ura in 1185.

ashikaga-yoshimasa.name: Ashikaga Yoshimasa
ashikaga-yoshimasa.summary: The eighth shogun of Japan's Ashikaga shogunate, ruling from 1443 to 1473; his actions led to the Onin War alongside a cultural flourishing that included the tea ceremony.

ashikaga-yoshimi.name: Ashikaga Yoshimi
ashikaga-yoshimi.summary: Brother of shogun Ashikaga Yoshimasa and his rival in the succession dispute (1439-1491) that led to the Onin War.

hino-tomiko.name: Hino Tomiko
hino-tomiko.summary: Wife of the eighth Ashikaga shōgun Yoshimasa and mother of the ninth (1440–1496), whose role in a succession dispute helped trigger the Ōnin War and the start of Japan's Sengoku period.

yamana-s-zen.name: Yamana Sōzen
yamana-s-zen.summary: Japanese daimyō (1404–1473), nicknamed 'the Red Monk' for his complexion, who fought the Hosokawa clan during the Ōnin War.

hosokawa-clan.name: Hosokawa Clan
hosokawa-clan.summary: A Japanese samurai clan descended from the Minamoto through the Ashikaga, which produced many officials of the Ashikaga shogunate and became one of the largest daimyo families of the Edo period.

takezaki-suenaga.name: Takezaki Suenaga
takezaki-suenaga.summary: Japanese retainer who fought in both Mongol invasions of Japan and commissioned an illustrated handscroll recording his battles (1246–1324).

kamakura.name: Kamakura
kamakura.summary: A Japanese city that served as the country's de facto capital from 1185 to 1333 as seat of the Kamakura shogunate, Japan's first military government.

tomoe-gozen.name: Tomoe Gozen
tomoe-gozen.summary: A legendary female samurai described in The Tale of the Heike as serving Minamoto no Yoshinaka during the Genpei War, though her historical existence is uncertain.

minamoto-no-yoshinaka.name: Minamoto no Yoshinaka
minamoto-no-yoshinaka.summary: A samurai lord (1154–1184), also called Kiso Yoshinaka, cousin and rival of shogun Minamoto no Yoritomo during the Genpei War, featured in the epic Tale of the Heike.

onna-musha.name: Onna-musha
onna-musha.summary: Term for female warriors of Japan's pre-modern samurai class who trained in weapons to defend their households and sometimes fought in battle; Tomoe Gozen is a famous example.

battle-of-awazu.name: Battle of Awazu
battle-of-awazu.summary: The final stand in 1184 of Minamoto no Yoshinaka, who died there with his foster brother Imai Kanehira after fleeing his cousin's pursuing army.

yamashiro-ikki.name: Yamashiro ikki
yamashiro-ikki.summary: A confederacy of local samurai and peasants who seized control of Yamashiro Province in 1485 after expelling two warring armies, ruling it independently until 1493.

hatakeyama-clan.name: Hatakeyama clan
hatakeyama-clan.summary: A Japanese samurai clan descended from the Taira and later linked to the Ashikaga lineage, whose rival branches fought for control of southern Yamashiro in the 15th century.

yamashiro-province.name: Yamashiro Province
yamashiro-province.summary: Historic province of Japan covering the area of modern Kyoto, seat of the imperial court from 794 and later of the Ashikaga shogunate.

kikuchi-takefusa.name: Kikuchi Takefusa
kikuchi-takefusa.summary: The 10th head of the Kikuchi clan of Higo Province, Japan, 1245 to 1298, famed for defending Japan during both Mongol invasions.

renga.name: Renga
renga.summary: A genre of Japanese collaborative linked poetry with alternating 5-7-5 and 7-7 syllable stanzas, elevated to a literary art by Nijō Yoshimoto in the 14th century.

otogi-z-shi.name: Otogi-zōshi
otogi-z-shi.summary: A group of roughly 350 unattributed illustrated Japanese prose narratives written mainly in the Muromachi period (1392–1573), a major genre of medieval Japanese literature.

noh.name: Noh
noh.summary: A major form of classical Japanese dance-drama performed since the 14th century, Japan's oldest major theater art still regularly staged, using masks and stylized gesture to tell stories of supernatural beings.

gunki-monogatari.name: Gunki monogatari
gunki-monogatari.summary: A category of Japanese war-tale literature written mainly in the Kamakura and Muromachi periods, focused on the civil wars fought between 1156 and 1568.

the-tale-of-the-heike.name: The Tale of the Heike
the-tale-of-the-heike.summary: An epic account, compiled before 1330, of the struggle between the Taira and Minamoto clans for control of Japan during the Genpei War (1180–1185); translated into English at least five times.

minamoto-clan.name: Minamoto clan
minamoto-clan.summary: A noble Japanese surname given to imperial family members excluded from succession from 814, whose most notable line founded the Kamakura and Ashikaga shogunates.

kamakura-period.name: Kamakura period
kamakura-period.summary: The period of Japanese history from 1185 to 1333 under the Kamakura shogunate, marked by the rise of the samurai warrior class and the start of feudalism.

samguk-sagi.name: Samguk sagi
samguk-sagi.summary: A history of Korea's Three Kingdoms completed in 1145 under King Injong of Goryeo; it is the oldest surviving Korean chronicle, compiled by the official Kim Pusik.

samguk-yusa.name: Samguk yusa
samguk-yusa.summary: A collection of Korean legends and historical accounts compiled by the Buddhist monk Il-yeon around 1280; it holds the earliest surviving record of the Dangun founding legend.

three-kingdoms-of-korea.name: Three Kingdoms of Korea
three-kingdoms-of-korea.summary: The era when the Korean peninsula was divided among the rival kingdoms of Goguryeo, Paekche and Silla, whose peoples became the Korean people.

silla.name: Silla
silla.summary: A Korean kingdom lasting from 57 BCE to 935 CE, one of the Three Kingdoms of Korea, which eventually conquered the other two and unified much of the peninsula.

hyangga.name: Hyangga
hyangga.summary: Poems written with Chinese characters during Korea's Unified Silla and early Goryeo periods; only a few dozen survive.

yongbi-ch-n-ga.name: Yongbiŏch'ŏn'ga
yongbi-ch-n-ga.summary: First work written in Hangul, published in 1447, an epic poem justifying the founding of the Joseon dynasty and the reigns of Sejong's predecessors.

akjang.name: Akjang
akjang.summary: The lyrics of Korean court music, most popular during the Joseon period of Korean history.

joseon.name: Joseon
joseon.summary: A Korean dynastic kingdom founded in 1392 by Taejo, lasting 505 years until 1897, which entrenched Confucian ideals and saw the height of classical Korean culture and science.

setsuwa.name: Setsuwa
setsuwa.summary: A Japanese literary genre of myths, legends, folktales and anecdotes rooted in oral tradition, told in plain language and divided into secular and Buddhist themes.

nihon-ry-iki.name: Nihon Ryōiki
nihon-ry-iki.summary: Japan's oldest collection of Buddhist setsuwa tales, written by the monk Kyōkai between 787 and 824 in three volumes.

imagawa-sadayo.name: Imagawa Ryōshun
imagawa-sadayo.summary: A Japanese poet and military commander (1326–1420) who served as constable of Kyūshū under the Ashikaga shogunate from 1371 to 1395.

ch-oe-yun-i.name: Ch'oe Yun-ŭi
ch-oe-yun-i.summary: A Korean inventor, politician and writer of the Goryeo period who compiled an official ceremonial text with 16 other scholars, establishing the rank system for officials' uniforms.

hwacha.name: Hwacha
hwacha.summary: A 15th-century Korean weapons cart that could fire up to 200 rocket-powered arrows at once, used against Japanese invasions in 1592 to 1598.

gangnido.name: Kangnido
gangnido.summary: A 1402 Korean world map by scholars Kwon Kun and Yi Hoe, the oldest surviving Korean world map, showing Africa, Europe, and Asia as far as Japan.

ch-oe-mus-n.name: Ch'oe Mu-sŏn
ch-oe-mus-n.summary: A medieval Korean chemist, inventor and military general (1330-1395) who obtained the gunpowder recipe from a Chinese merchant and invented gunpowder weapons to fight coastal pirates.

u-of-goryeo.name: U of Goryeo
u-of-goryeo.summary: 32nd king of Goryeo, Korea, ruling from 1374 to 1388 as the only son of King Gongmin.

sin-gij-n.name: Sin'gijŏn
sin-gij-n.summary: A Korean fire arrow rocket used during the Joseon Dynasty (1392–1897), often launched in multiples from a hwacha rocket launcher.

taejong-of-joseon.name: Taejong of Joseon
taejong-of-joseon.summary: Third monarch of Joseon (1367–1422) and father of Sejong the Great, a major figure in establishing the dynasty who took the throne from his brother.

wokou.name: Wokou
wokou.summary: Pirates known as 'Japanese pirates' or 'dwarf pirates' who raided the coasts of China and Korea from the 13th to 17th centuries, drawn from various East Asian peoples.

johannes-gutenberg.name: Johannes Gutenberg
johannes-gutenberg.summary: German inventor (c. 1393–1468) of the movable-type printing press, whose innovations in type-casting and oil-based ink enabled the Gutenberg Bible and are credited with sparking an information revolution across Europe.

taejo-of-joseon.name: Taejo of Joseon
taejo-of-joseon.summary: Founder of the Joseon dynasty, who took the throne in 1392 after overthrowing Goryeo, ruled six years, and was later honored as Emperor Ko.

heiji-rebellion.name: Heiji rebellion
heiji-rebellion.summary: A short 1160 civil war between rival subjects of Emperor Go-Shirakawa over political power, following the Hōgen Rebellion and seen as a precursor to a wider civil war.

tributary-system-of-china.name: Imperial Chinese tributary system
tributary-system-of-china.summary: A network of relations centered on China in which other states sent envoys who kowtowed to the Chinese emperor to acknowledge his superiority in exchange for trade and diplomatic ties.

neo-confucianism.name: Neo-Confucianism
neo-confucianism.summary: A revival of Confucianism as an ethical, social and religious system that dominated Chinese philosophy from the 13th to 19th century, developed under Zhu Xi during the Song dynasty.

liao-dynasty.name: Liao dynasty
liao-dynasty.summary: A Khitan-led imperial dynasty of China (916–1125) that at its height ruled Manchuria, Mongolia, northern Korea, and parts of Siberia and North China.

hans-bielenstein.name: Hans Bielenstein
hans-bielenstein.summary: A Swedish sinologist (1920–2015) and Columbia University professor who specialized in the history of the Han dynasty.

hyeonjong-of-goryeo.name: Hyeonjong of Goryeo
hyeonjong-of-goryeo.summary: 8th ruler of Korea's Goryeo dynasty, 992 to 1031, who fought two wars against the Khitan Liao dynasty and is remembered as one of Korea's greatest leaders.

sejong-the-great.name: Sejong the Great
sejong-the-great.summary: Fourth monarch of Joseon, ruling Korea from 1418 to 1450 and widely regarded as its greatest king, remembered for creating the Hangul alphabet and advances in science and agriculture.

nobi.name: Nobi
nobi.summary: The slave class of Korea's Goryeo and Joseon dynasties, its lowest legal rank, whose members could be bought, sold or gifted and who made up over 30% of the population at their peak.

tendai.name: Tendai
tendai.summary: A Mahayana Buddhist school founded in Japan in 806 by the monk Saicho, based on Mount Hiei, that became a dominant Buddhist tradition by the Kamakura period.

shingon-buddhism.name: Shingon Buddhism
shingon-buddhism.summary: A major school of Japanese Esoteric Buddhism founded by the monk Kūkai (774–835) after he studied in Tang China, centered at Mount Kōya.

pure-land-buddhism.name: Pure Land Buddhism
pure-land-buddhism.summary: A broad branch of Mahayana Buddhism, widespread in East Asia, focused on achieving rebirth in a Buddha's 'pure land,' where enlightenment is far easier to attain.

nichiren-buddhism.name: Nichiren Buddhism
nichiren-buddhism.summary: A branch of Mahayana Buddhism based on the teachings of the 13th-century Japanese priest Nichiren, centred on faith in the Lotus Sutra and chanting Nam Myoho Renge Kyo.

unified-silla.name: Unified Silla
unified-silla.summary: Period of the Korean kingdom of Silla after it conquered Goguryeo in 668 CE, unifying the central and southern Korean peninsula until it fell to Goryeo in 935.

zhu-xi.name: Zhu Xi
zhu-xi.summary: A Chinese philosopher, historian and politician (1130–1200) of the Southern Song dynasty, the leading figure of Neo-Confucianism, whose commentaries were core exam texts until 1905.

song-dynasty.name: Song dynasty
song-dynasty.summary: Imperial Chinese dynasty that ruled from 960 to 1279, later split into a northern and southern period after losing northern China to the Jurchen Jin dynasty, before its conquest by the Mongols.

heian-period.name: Heian period
heian-period.summary: The last division of classical Japanese history (794–1185), a peak of imperial court art and literature even though real power lay with the Fujiwara clan.

godai-japanese-philosophy.name: Godai
godai-japanese-philosophy.summary: The five elements in Japanese Buddhist thought - earth, water, fire, wind and void - derived from Indian Buddhism and linked to esoteric teachings from the eleventh century.

ninjutsu.name: Ninjutsu
ninjutsu.summary: Techniques and skills used by ninja, covert operatives and irregular-warfare specialists in pre-modern Japan, some recorded in surviving ninja scrolls.

eisai.name: Eisai
eisai.summary: A Japanese Buddhist priest (1141–1215) credited with founding the Rinzai school of Zen Buddhism after studying in China, and with popularizing green tea in Japan.

hirado-nagasaki.name: Hirado
hirado-nagasaki.summary: A port city in Nagasaki Prefecture, Japan, that served as a key gateway for foreign trade with Europe in the 16th–17th centuries and today has about 28,000 residents.

my-e.name: Myōe
my-e.summary: A Japanese Buddhist monk (1173–1232) of the Kamakura period, also known as Kōben, and a contemporary of the monks Jōkei and Hōnen.

k-zan-ji.name: Kōzan-ji
k-zan-ji.summary: A Shingon Buddhist temple in Kyoto founded by the monk Myōe (1173–1232), renowned for its treasures including 12th–13th century ink paintings, part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

uji.name: Uji
uji.summary: A city on the southern outskirts of Kyoto, Japan, between the ancient capitals of Nara and Kyoto, long renowned for producing high-quality tea.

nanboku-ch-period.name: Nanbokuchō period
nanboku-ch-period.summary: A period in Japanese history (1336–1392) when rival Northern and Southern imperial courts competed for legitimacy during the Muromachi shogunate's formative years.

enj-ji.name: Enjō-ji
enj-ji.summary: Shingon Buddhist temple in northeast Nara, Japan, with buildings and images designated National Treasures and late-Heian gardens named a Place of Scenic Beauty.

shoin.name: Shoin
shoin.summary: A drawing-room or study style in Japanese architecture developed during the Muromachi period; its standardized tatami-mat flooring shaped the proportions of later buildings.
